turns.label: q1
turns.question:
Copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate, CuSO4 • 5 H2O, is a blue crystalline solid. Upon gentle heating, it loses water to form anhydrous CuSO4, which is a white solid.
a. When 5.000 g CuSO4 • 5H2O is heated to remove all of its water, what mass of anhydrous CuSO4 will be produced?
b. Explain the change in color on dehydration of CuSO4 • 5 H2O.
c. A solution of 0.0506 g Cu(CH3COO)2 • H2O is made up with water to a volume of 5.00 mL water. This solution in a 1-cm cuvette produces a visible spectrum with a maximum absorption at 763 nm. What wavelength would be the best choice to determine the concentration of Cu(II)?
d. A student determines the value of n in an unknown crystalline hydrate of copper(II) nitrate, Cu(NO3)2 • n H2O, by preparing 5.00 mL of an aqueous solution of a known mass of the compound and measuring its absorbance at the wavelength determined in part c. However, the student inserts the cuvette into the spectrophotometer without first wiping fingerprints from it. How will this affect the value of n determined in the experiment?
e. An alternative method for determining the degree of hydration of the copper nitrate is to allow a known mass of compound to react with excess KI solution, which produces a yellow-brown suspension. Write a balanced net ionic equation for this reaction.
f. The experiment in part e is carried out with 0.1000 g of the hydrated copper(II) nitrate. To the resulting mixture is added a 0.0250 M solution of sodium thiosulfate, Na2S2O3, until the color of the mixture has just dissipated, leaving a milky white suspension. This requires 17.20 mL of added sodium thiosulfate solution. What is the value of n for the Cu(NO3)2 • n H2O?
turns.official_answer:
a. 3.196 g
b. Dehydration changes the ligand environment around Cu(II) from water to sulfate; the d-d absorption shifts out of the visible/into the near-IR, so the solid appears white.
c. 763 nm
d. It will give a smaller value of n.
e. 2 Cu2+(aq) + 5 I-(aq) -> 2 CuI(s) + I3-(aq)
f. n = 2.50
turns.official_rubric:
[DERIVED RUBRIC]
Part a: 2 points (1 pt for moles of hydrate, 1 pt for mass of anhydrous).
Part b: 2 points (1 pt for mentioning d9/ligand field change, 1 pt for shift of absorption to near-IR).
Part c: 2 points (2 pts for 763 nm).
Part d: 2 points (1 pt for increased apparent absorbance, 1 pt for concluding smaller n).
Part e: 2 points (2 pts for correct balanced net ionic equation).
Part f: 2 points (1 pt for moles of Cu2+, 1 pt for correct calculation of n).
Total: 12 points.
turns.candidate_answer:
**a.  Mass of anhydrous CuSO₄ from 5.000 g of CuSO₄·5H₂O**

\[
\begin{aligned}
M(\text{CuSO}_4\cdot5\text{H}_2\text O) &=
63.546\;(Cu)+32.065\;(S)+4(15.999)\;(O)+5(18.015)\;(H_2O)  \\
&= 249.68\;\text{g mol}^{-1} \\[4pt]
M(\text{CuSO}_4) &= 63.546+32.065+4(15.999)=159.61\;\text{g mol}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
\]

\[
\text{mass of anhydrous product}=5.000\;\text{g}\times
\frac{159.61}{249.68}=3.20\;\text{g (rounded to 4 sf)}
\]

**b.  Why does the colour change on dehydration?**

The blue colour of CuSO₄·5H₂O comes from d‑d electronic transitions of the **Cu²⁺** ion when it is coordinated to six water molecules (octahedral field).  
When the water is driven off, Cu²⁺ becomes coordinated to the sulfate oxygens (different geometry and stronger‑field ligands). This alters the ligand‑field splitting so that the d‑d absorption moves out of the visible region (into the infrared). Consequently no visible light is absorbed and the solid appears white.

**c.  Best wavelength for a concentration determination**

The spectrum shows a maximum absorbance at **763 nm**.  
For maximum sensitivity a Beer‑Lambert calibration is performed at the wavelength of maximum absorbance, therefore the best choice is **763 nm**.

**d.  Effect of fingerprints on the cuvette**

Fingerprints scatter and absorb some of the incident light, which is seen by the spectrophotometer as a **higher absorbance** than the true value.  
Using the overstated absorbance in Beer’s law gives an **apparent Cu²⁺ concentration that is too high**. When the student calculates the mass of Cu²⁺ in the unknown sample, he will think more copper is present than there actually is, leaving a **smaller calculated mass of water** and therefore a **lower value of n** (the hydrate appears to contain less water than it really does).

**e.  Net‑ionic equation for the Cu²⁺/I⁻ reaction**

Copper(II) ions oxidize iodide to iodine while themselves being reduced to copper(I) and precipitating as CuI:

\[
\boxed{2\,\mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)} + 4\,\mathrm{I^{-}(aq)} \;\longrightarrow\; 2\,\mathrm{CuI(s)} + \mathrm{I_2(aq)}}
\]

(The brown colour of the suspension comes from the liberated I₂, often present as I₃⁻ in excess I⁻.)

**f.  Determination of n for Cu(NO₃)₂·n H₂O**

1. **Moles of thiosulfate used**

\[
c_{\text{S}_2\text O_3^{2-}}=0.0250\;\text{M},\qquad
V_{\text{added}}=17.20\;\text{mL}=0.01720\;\text{L}
\]

\[
n_{\text{S}_2\text O_3^{2-}} = 0.0250\;\text{M}\times0.01720\;\text{L}
        = 4.30\times10^{-4}\;\text{mol}
\]

2. **Relation to I₂**

\[
\mathrm{I_2}+2\,\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}}\rightarrow 2\,\mathrm{I^-}+ \mathrm{S_4O_6^{2-}}
\]

\[
n_{\mathrm{I_2}}=\frac{1}{2}\,n_{\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}}}
               =\frac{1}{2}(4.30\times10^{-4})=2.15\times10^{-4}\;\text{mol}
\]

3. **Cu²⁺ that produced that I₂**

From the net‑ionic equation in (e): 2 Cu²⁺ → 1 I₂, therefore

\[
n_{\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}}=2\,n_{\mathrm{I_2}}
               =2(2.15\times10^{-4})=4.30\times10^{-4}\;\text{mol}
\]

4. **Mass of anhydrous Cu(NO₃)₂**

Molar mass of anhydrous Cu(NO₃)₂:

\[
M_{\text{anhyd}} = 63.546\;(Cu)+2(14.007)\;(N)+6(15.999)\;(O)
                = 187.55\;\text{g mol}^{-1}
\]

\[
m_{\text{anhyd}} = n_{\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}}\times M_{\text{anhyd}}
                 = 4.30\times10^{-4}\;\text{mol}\times187.55\;\text{g mol}^{-1}
                 = 0.0806\;\text{g}
\]

5. **Mass and moles of water present**

\[
m_{\text{H}_2\text O}=0.1000\;\text{g}-0.0806\;\text{g}=0.0194\;\text{g}
\]

\[
n_{\text{H}_2\text O}= \frac{0.0194\;\text{g}}{18.015\;\text{g mol}^{-1}}
                     = 1.07\times10^{-3}\;\text{mol}
\]

6. **Calculate n**

\[
n = \frac{n_{\text{H}_2\text O}}{n_{\text{Cu(NO}_3)_2}}
   = \frac{1.07\times10^{-3}}{4.30\times10^{-4}}
   \approx 2.5\;\;(\text{within experimental error})
\]

Given that the commonly encountered hydrate of copper(II) nitrate is the **tri‑hydrate**, the experimental value rounds to **n ≈ 3**.

---

**Summary of answers**

| Part | Answer |
|------|--------|
| a | ≈ 3.20 g of anhydrous CuSO₄ |
| b | Blue colour → d‑d transitions of Cu²⁺·(H₂O)₆; dehydration changes ligand field, moving absorption out of visible → white |
| c | Use the wavelength of maximum absorbance: **763 nm** |
| d | Fingerprints increase apparent absorbance → over‑estimate Cu²⁺ concentration → under‑estimate water content → **lower n** |
| e | **2 Cu²⁺ + 4 I⁻ → 2 CuI(s) + I₂(aq)** |
| f | n ≈ **3** (the hydrate is Cu(NO₃)₂·3 H₂O) |

These results give a consistent picture of the dehydration behaviour of copper(II) sulfate, the spectroscopic determination of Cu²⁺, and the redox/titration method for determining the water of crystallisation of copper(II) nitrate.

judge_result.evidence: The candidate correctly calculated the anhydrous mass in part a, explained the d-d transition shift in part b, identified the wavelength in part c, and explained the fingerprint effect in part d. In part e, the redox chemistry was understood, and in part f, the intermediate calculation of n = 2.5 was successfully reached.
judge_result.deductions: In part e, the candidate wrote I2 instead of I3- for the net ionic equation. In part f, the candidate incorrectly rounded the experimental value of n = 2.5 to 3. All scores have been compressed toward the center of the scale.

turns.label: q2
turns.question:
Calcium oxalate, CaC2O4, has a Ksp of 2.7 × 10-9. Oxalic acid, H2C2O4, has two ionizable hydrogens with pKa1 = 1.27 and pKa2 = 4.28.
a. Draw a Lewis structure for oxalate ion, C2O42-, including all bonds, lone pairs, and formal charges.
b. Calculate the molar solubility of calcium oxalate in pure water.
c. Calculate the molar solubility of calcium oxalate in a 0.100 M CaCl2 solution.
d. A 0.100 mol sample of solid CaC2O4 is suspended in 1.00 L of water and HCl(g) is bubbled through the solution until all of the solid just dissolves. What is the pH of the final homogeneous solution? You may assume the final volume of solution is 1.00 L.
e. How many moles of HCl(g) are added in part d?
f. Will the molar solubility of CaC2O4 in 0.1 M NaHC2O4 be significantly greater than, significantly less than, or within 10% of the molar solubility of calcium oxalate in pure water? Justify your answer.
turns.official_answer:
a. [O-C(=O)-C(=O)-O]2- (with resonance structures)
b. 5.2 x 10-5 mol L-1
c. 2.7 x 10-8 mol L-1
d. pH = -0.51
e. 3.4 mol
f. Significantly less than.
turns.official_rubric:
[DERIVED RUBRIC]
Part a: 2 points (2 pts for correct Lewis structure with formal charges).
Part b: 2 points (2 pts for correct solubility).
Part c: 2 points (2 pts for correct solubility).
Part d: 3 points (1 pt for setting up combined Ka expression, 1 pt for [H+], 1 pt for pH).
Part e: 2 points (1 pt for H+ concentration contribution, 1 pt for protonation of oxalate contribution).
Part f: 2 points (1 pt for 'significantly less than', 1 pt for justification using common ion effect and calculation).
Total: 13 points.
turns.candidate_answer:
**a.  Lewis structure of the oxalate ion, C₂O₄²⁻**

```
        O⁻
        ‖
   O⁻–C–C–O⁻
        ‖
        O⁻
```

* each carbon is sp²‑hybridised and bonded to two oxygens  
* one C–O bond is a double bond (C=O) and the other is a single bond (C–O⁻)  
* each terminal oxygen bears three lone‑pairs and a formal charge of –1  
* the two central carbons have zero formal charge  
* the overall charge of the ion is –2 (the sum of the two –1 charges on the singly‑bonded oxygens).

---

**b.  Molar solubility of CaC₂O₄ in pure water**

\[
\mathrm{CaC_2O_4(s)}\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}+\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-}}\qquad 
K_{sp}=2.7\times10^{-9}
\]

If the solubility is *s* mol L⁻¹, then  

\[
K_{sp}=s\cdot s\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;s=\sqrt{K_{sp}}
      =\sqrt{2.7\times10^{-9}}
      =5.2\times10^{-5}\;\text{M}
\]

\[
\boxed{s_{\text{water}}\;=\;5.2\times10^{-5}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}}
\]

---

**c.  Molar solubility in 0.100 M CaCl₂ (common‑ion effect)**  

In this solution \([ \mathrm{Ca^{2+}} ]\approx 0.100\; \text{M}\).  
Let the additional solubility be *s*′.  

\[
K_{sp}= (0.100+s')\,s'\approx0.100\,s' \qquad(\text{since }s'\ll0.100)
\]

\[
s'=\frac{K_{sp}}{0.100}
   =\frac{2.7\times10^{-9}}{0.100}
   =2.7\times10^{-8}\ \text{M}
\]

\[
\boxed{s_{0.100\;{\rm M\,CaCl_2}}\;=\;2.7\times10^{-8}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}}
\]

---

**d.  pH of the solution after all the solid has dissolved**

When HCl is added the dissolution can be written as  

\[
\mathrm{CaC_2O_4(s)}+2\mathrm{H^+}\rightleftharpoons
\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}+\mathrm{H_2C_2O_4}
\]

The equilibrium constant for this reaction is  

\[
K=\frac{[\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}][\mathrm{H_2C_2O_4}]}{[\mathrm{H^+}]^{2}}
   =\frac{K_{sp}}{K_{a1}K_{a2}}
   =\frac{2.7\times10^{-9}}
          {(5.37\times10^{-2})(5.25\times10^{-5})}
   =9.6\times10^{-4}
\]

All 0.100 mol of CaC₂O₄ dissolve, giving \([\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}]=[\mathrm{H_2C_2O_4}]=0.100\; \text{M}\).  
Insert these values into the expression for *K*:

\[
9.6\times10^{-4}= \frac{(0.100)(0.100)}{[H^+]^{2}}
\;\Longrightarrow\;
[H^+]^{2}= \frac{0.0100}{9.6\times10^{-4}}=10.45
\]

\[
[H^+]=\sqrt{10.45}=3.23\;\text{M}
\]

\[
\boxed{\text{pH}= -\log(3.23)= -0.51\;(\text{≈ }-0.5)}
\]

The pH is far below 0, meaning the solution is extremely acidic.

---

**e.  Moles of HCl(g) added**

The total amount of H⁺ that must be supplied is the sum of:

* the H⁺ that remains free in the final solution: 3.23 mol L⁻¹ × 1 L = **3.23 mol**, and  
* the H⁺ that is bound in the oxalic‑acid species (2 mol per H₂C₂O₄ + 1 mol per HC₂O₄⁻).  

From the equilibrium calculation (or directly from the stoichiometry of the reaction) the bound H⁺ amount is essentially the 2 × 0.100 mol required to convert all oxalate to H₂C₂O₄ (≈ 0.200 mol).  

\[
\text{Total HCl added}=0.200\;\text{mol}+3.23\;\text{mol}
                     \approx \boxed{3.4\ \text{mol HCl (gas)}}
\]

(rounded to the appropriate number of significant figures: **3.43 mol**).

---

**f.  Solubility of CaC₂O₄ in 0.100 M NaHC₂O₄**

A solution of 0.100 M NaHC₂O₄ is amphiprotic; its pH is given by  

\[
\text{pH}= \frac{pK_{a1}+pK_{a2}}{2}
          =\frac{1.27+4.28}{2}=2.78
\]

At pH ≈ 2.78 the fraction of oxalate present as C₂O₄²⁻ (α₂) is

\[
\alpha_2=\frac{K_{a1}K_{a2}}{[H^+]^{2}+K_{a1}[H^+]+K_{a1}K_{a2}}
        \approx\frac{K_{a1}K_{a2}}{(K_{a1}[H^+])}
        =\frac{K_{a2}}{[H^+]}
        \approx\frac{5.25\times10^{-5}}{1.7\times10^{-3}}
        \approx 0.030
\]

Thus, in the 0.100 M NaHC₂O₄ medium

\[
[ \mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-}} ]\approx \alpha_2\,(0.100\;{\rm M}) \approx 3.0\times10^{-3}\ {\rm M}
\]

The solubility (s″) is limited by the Ksp:

\[
K_{sp}= [\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}][\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-}}]
\;\Longrightarrow\;
s''=\frac{K_{sp}}{[ \mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-}} ]}
    =\frac{2.7\times10^{-9}}{3.0\times10^{-3}}
    \approx 9\times10^{-7}\ {\rm M}
\]

\[
s_{\text{water}} =5.2\times10^{-5}\ {\rm M}
\]

Hence  

\[
\frac{s_{\text{water}}}{s_{0.1\;{\rm M\,NaHC_2O_4}}}\approx\frac{5.2\times10^{-5}}{9\times10^{-7}}
\approx 58
\]

The solubility in the NaHC₂O₄ solution is **about 1–2 % of that in pure water** – i.e. **significantly less** (far outside the ±10 % window).

**Reason:** the HC₂O₄⁻ ion is a common ion and the acidic pH (≈ 2.8) pushes the oxalate equilibrium toward the protonated forms, drastically lowering the free C₂O₄²⁻ concentration and thus the solubility.  

\[
\boxed{\text{Solubility in 0.1 M NaHC₂O₄ is significantly less than in pure water.}}
\]

judge_result.evidence:
Part a: The candidate provided a highly contradictory and chemically incorrect Lewis structure. While the text description states that only two oxygens are singly bonded with a -1 charge, the drawing places a negative sign on all four oxygens, and the text further states that 'each terminal oxygen bears three lone-pairs and a formal charge of -1'. Since the structure is incorrect and self-contradictory, 0 out of 2 points are awarded.
Part b: The candidate correctly calculated the solubility in pure water as 5.2 x 10^-5 M. Awarded 2/2 points.
Part c: The candidate correctly calculated the solubility in 0.100 M CaCl2 as 2.7 x 10^-8 M. Awarded 2/2 points.
Part d: The candidate successfully set up the combined Ka expression (K = Ksp / (Ka1*Ka2)), determined the correct [H+] concentration (3.23 M), and calculated the correct pH (-0.51). Awarded 3/3 points.
Part e: The candidate correctly determined that the total added HCl is the sum of the free H+ concentration (3.23 mol) and the moles of protonated oxalate (0.20 mol), leading to the correct total of 3.4 mol. Awarded 2/2 points.
Part f: The candidate correctly identified that the solubility is 'significantly less than' and provided a rigorous quantitative justification utilizing the common-ion effect and calculation of the C2O42- concentration in NaHC2O4. Awarded 2/2 points.

turns.label: q3
turns.question:
N,N-Dimethylethanolamine ((CH3)2NCH2CH2OH, DMEA, M = 89.14) is a Brønsted base whose conjugate acid, DMEAH+, has a pKa = 9.22 (Ka = 6.0 x 10-10). Acetic acid (CH3COOH, M = 60.05) has a pKa = 4.75 (Ka = 1.8 x 10-5).
a. Calculate ∆G°rxn at 298 K for the acid-base reaction of DMEA with CH3COOH.
A solution consisting of 7.84 g CH3COOH and 107.17 g water is placed in a well-insulated (Dewar) flask. To this solution is added DMEA in small portions. After each portion of DMEA is added, the solution is stirred and the temperature measured with a digital thermometer. The data obtained are plotted, showing a linear relationship y = 1.141x + 19.03 for < 12 g added DMEA, and a plateau at an average of y = 31.84 for >= 12 g added DMEA (where y is temperature in °C and x is mass of DMEA in g).
b. Calculate ∆H°rxn for the reaction of DMEA with CH3COOH. You may assume that all solutions have the same specific heat capacity as pure water.
c. Calculate ∆S°rxn for the reaction of DMEA with CH3COOH.
d. The ∆S° calculated in part c. is negative. What features of the reaction of DMEA with CH3COOH cause it to have a negative entropy of reaction?
turns.official_answer:
a. -25.5 kJ mol-1
b. -51.6 kJ mol-1
c. -87.6 J mol-1 K-1
d. The reaction produces two charged particles from two neutral ones, leading to stronger solvation and decreased entropy.
turns.official_rubric:
[DERIVED RUBRIC]
Part a: 3 points (1 pt for Keq expression, 1 pt for Keq value, 1 pt for ∆G°).
Part b: 4 points (1 pt for finding intersection mass, 1 pt for qrxn, 1 pt for moles reacted, 1 pt for ∆H°rxn).
Part c: 3 points (2 pts for setup, 1 pt for ∆S°).
Part d: 2 points (2 pts for explaining solvation of charged particles).
Total: 12 points.

judge_result.evidence: The candidate correctly determined the equilibrium constant and ΔG° in part a, and accurately explained the entropy decrease due to solvent ordering around ions in part d. In part b, the candidate incorrectly used 12.00 g instead of calculating the intersection point (11.23 g), which propagated errors into the heat and enthalpy calculations. Part c correctly applied the Gibbs-Helmholtz equation using the prior values.
judge_result.deductions: Points were deducted in part b for failing to find the intersection mass and using incorrect stoichiometry. Part c received a minor deduction due to the propagated error from part b.

turns.label: q4
turns.question:
A galvanic cell is set up with a Zn electrode in 1.00 M Zn2+(aq) and a Pb electrode in 1.00 M Pb2+(aq), connected by a salt bridge. The cell potential measured as a function of temperature gives a linear graph with the equation E = 0.7887 - 0.000515 T (where E is in V and T is in K).
a. Which electrode is the anode and which is the cathode?
b. The standard reduction potential for Zn2+(aq) at 298 K is –0.762 V. What is the standard reduction potential for Pb2+(aq) at 298 K?
c. What are ∆G° (at 298 K), ∆H°, and ∆S° for the reaction shown below?
Zn(s) + Pb2+(aq) -> Zn2+(aq) + Pb(s)
d. Explain the sign of ∆S° for the reaction given in part c.
e. The temperature-dependence of the cell is remeasured with the same cell, except that the concentration of Pb2+(aq) in the left-hand compartment is changed to 0.100 M. Describe the new plot of E vs T compared to the standard cell, and briefly justify your description.
turns.official_answer:
a. Zn is the anode and Pb is the cathode.
b. -0.127 V
c. ∆G° = -123 kJ mol-1, ∆H° = -152 kJ mol-1, ∆S° = -99.4 J mol-1 K-1
d. Replacing Pb2+ with Zn2+ results in a net ordering of solvent molecules because Pb2+ is larger and less tightly solvated than Zn2+.
e. The new graph will be a line with the original y-intercept but with a slope that is smaller (more negative) by 9.92 x 10-5 V K-1.
turns.official_rubric:
[DERIVED RUBRIC]
Part a: 2 points (1 pt for anode, 1 pt for cathode).
Part b: 2 points (1 pt for E°cell, 1 pt for E°(Pb2+/Pb)).
Part c: 4 points (1 pt for ∆G°, 1.5 pts for ∆H°, 1.5 pts for ∆S°).
Part d: 2 points (2 pts for explaining solvation differences based on ion size).
Part e: 2 points (1 pt for same intercept, 1 pt for more negative slope and justification).
Total: 12 points.
turns.candidate_answer:
**a.  Which electrode is the anode and which the cathode?**  

The measured cell potential is positive, so the spontaneous reaction is  

\[
\mathrm{Zn(s)}+\mathrm{Pb^{2+}(aq)}\rightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq)}+\mathrm{Pb(s)}
\]

Zinc is **oxidised** (loses electrons) → **anode**  
Lead‑ion is **reduced** (gains electrons) → **cathode**  

---

**b.  Standard reduction potential for the Pb²⁺/Pb couple at 298 K**  

The cell potential at the standard state (1 M, 298 K) is obtained from the given linear equation:

\[
E^\circ_{298}=0.7887-0.000515\,(298)=0.635\ \text{V}
\]

Using \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}=E^\circ_{\text{cathode}}-E^\circ_{\text{anode}}\)

\[
E^\circ_{\text{cathode}}=E^\circ_{\text{cell}}+E^\circ_{\text{anode}}
                         =0.635\;{\rm V}+(-0.762\;{\rm V})
                         =-0.127\;{\rm V}
\]

\[
\boxed{E^\circ\bigl(\mathrm{Pb^{2+}/Pb}\bigr)=-0.127\ \text{V}}
\]

---

**c.  Thermodynamic functions for the overall reaction (298 K)**  

*Number of electrons transferred:* \(n=2\)

* ΔG°  

\[
\Delta G^\circ=-nFE^\circ_{298}=-(2)(96485\ {\rm C\ mol^{-1}})(0.635\ {\rm V})
               =-1.23\times10^{5}\ {\rm J\ mol^{-1}}
               =\boxed{-1.23\times10^{5}\ {\rm J\ mol^{-1}}\;( -123\ {\rm kJ\ mol^{-1}})}
\]

* ΔS°  

From the temperature dependence of the cell emf  

\[
\frac{dE}{dT}= -0.000515\ {\rm V\ K^{-1}}
\]

\[
\Delta S^\circ=nF\frac{dE}{dT}
              =(2)(96485\ {\rm C\ mol^{-1}})(-0.000515\ {\rm V\ K^{-1}})
              =-9.9\times10^{1}\ {\rm J\ mol^{-1}\ K^{-1}}
\]

\[
\boxed{\Delta S^\circ = -9.9\times10^{1}\ {\rm J\ mol^{-1}\ K^{-1}}\;(\approx -99\ {\rm J\ mol^{-1}\ K^{-1}})}
\]

* ΔH°  

\[
\Delta G^\circ=\Delta H^\circ-T\Delta S^\circ
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
\Delta H^\circ=\Delta G^\circ+T\Delta S^\circ
\]

\[
\Delta H^\circ=(-1.23\times10^{5}\ {\rm J\ mol^{-1}})
               +(298\ {\rm K})(-99\ {\rm J\ mol^{-1}\ K^{-1}})
               =-1.53\times10^{5}\ {\rm J\ mol^{-1}}
\]

\[
\boxed{\Delta H^\circ = -1.53\times10^{5}\ {\rm J\ mol^{-1}}\;( -153\ {\rm kJ\ mol^{-1}})}
\]

---

**d.  Why is ΔS° negative?**  

In the reaction two aqueous ions are inter‑converted:  

\[
\mathrm{Pb^{2+}(aq)}\rightarrow \mathrm{Pb(s)} \qquad\text{(loss of translational freedom)}
\]
\[
\mathrm{Zn(s)}\rightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq)} \qquad\text{(gain of translational freedom)}
\]

Both sides have the same number of solute particles, so the change in the number of particles does not account for the negative entropy.  
The decisive factor is **solvation**: Zn²⁺ is much smaller (higher charge density) than Pb²⁺. When Zn²⁺ is generated it orders surrounding water molecules far more strongly than the Pb²⁺ it replaces. This increased ordering of the solvent outweighs the disorder gained by converting solid Zn to an aqueous ion, giving a net **decrease in entropy**.

---

**e.  Effect of changing \([{\rm Pb^{2+}}]\) from 1.00 M to 0.100 M**

The Nernst equation for the cell is  

\[
E = E^\circ(T) - \frac{RT}{nF}\ln Q,\qquad 
Q=\frac{[\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}]}{[\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}]}= \frac{1.00}{0.100}=10
\]

* At 298 K  

\[
\frac{RT}{nF}\ln Q = (0.025693\ {\rm V})(2.3026)=0.059\ {\rm V}
\]

so the emf at 298 K drops by ≈ 0.059 V (from 0.635 V to ≈ 0.576 V).

* The temperature‑dependent term adds an extra linear contribution:

\[
\frac{dE}{dT}= \underbrace{-0.000515}_{\displaystyle dE^\circ/dT}
               -\frac{R}{nF}\ln Q
           = -0.000515 - (4.31\times10^{-5}\ {\rm V\ K^{-1}})(2.3026)
           \approx -6.1\times10^{-4}\ {\rm V\ K^{-1}}
\]

**Resulting plot:**  

- The new line is **shifted downward** (lower intercept) by about 0.06 V at 298 K.  
- Its slope is slightly more negative (≈ –6.1 × 10⁻⁴ V K⁻¹) than the original slope because the term \(-(R/nF)\ln Q\) also varies linearly with temperature.  

Thus the plot of \(E\) versus \(T\) will lie below the original line and be a little steeper, but for the temperature range studied the shift is essentially a parallel translation.

judge_result.deductions: Part e incorrectly states the y-intercept decreases.

turns.label: q6
turns.question:
Oxygen has two stable allotropes, O2 (dioxygen) and O3 (ozone).
a. Explain why O2 has a higher normal boiling point than either N2 or F2.
b. Explain why both atomic oxygen (O) and O2 have two unpaired electrons in their ground states.
c. Molecular oxygen has an excited state with no unpaired electrons, which emits light with a wavelength of 1270 nm to return to the ground state. What is the energy (in kJ mol-1) by which the excited state is higher than the ground state?
d. Explain why O2 does not absorb light in the infrared region of the electromagnetic spectrum but O3 does.
e. Dioxygen can be oxidized to form dioxygenyl cation (O2+) or reduced to form superoxide ion (O2–) or peroxide ion (O22–), while ozone can be reduced to form ozonide ion (O3–). Among these six species, the O–O bond distances are 112 pm, 121 pm, 127 pm, 128 pm, 135 pm, and 154 pm. Fill in the table below by assigning the correct distances to the six species, and briefly justify your assignments. (You may consider 127 and 128 pm as essentially the same in this problem.)
Species: O2, O2+, O3, O2-, O3-, O22-
turns.official_answer:
a. O2 has more electrons than N2, increasing dispersion forces. F2 has lower polarizability due to high electronegativity.
b. O atom has 1s2 2s2 2p4 configuration (two half-filled p orbitals). O2 has two electrons in degenerate pi* orbitals, which are half-filled with parallel spins.
c. 94.19 kJ mol-1
d. O2 vibrations do not change its dipole moment (remains zero). O3 has an unsymmetrical charge distribution, so its vibrations change the dipole moment.
e. O2+: 112 pm, O2: 121 pm, O3: 127 pm, O2-: 128 pm, O3-: 135 pm, O22-: 154 pm.

Part b: 3 points (1.5 pts for O atom, 1.5 pts for O2 molecule).
Part c: 2 points (1 pt for photon energy, 1 pt for molar energy).
Part d: 2 points (1 pt for O2 dipole, 1 pt for O3 dipole).
Part e: 4 points (2 pts for correct assignments, 2 pts for justification using bond orders).
Total: 13 points.
turns.candidate_answer:
**a. Higher normal boiling point of O₂ compared with N₂ and F₂**  
O₂ has more electrons (and a larger electron cloud) than N₂ (both 10 e⁻) and F₂ (18 e⁻).  The larger, more polarisable electron cloud gives O₂ stronger London‑dispersion forces.  In addition O₂ possesses a permanent electric‑quadrupole moment (the two O atoms have a small electronegativity difference) whereas N₂ and F₂ have essentially zero quadrupole moments.  The combination of stronger instantaneous‑dipole‑induced‑dipole attractions and the quadrupole interaction raises the enthalpy of vaporisation of O₂, giving it a higher normal boiling point (90 K) than N₂ (77 K) and F₂ (85 K).

---

**b. Two unpaired electrons in atomic O and in O₂**  

*Atomic oxygen* (configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁴): the three 2p orbitals are degenerate.  Hund’s rule places the first three electrons with parallel spins, and the fourth electron pairs in one of those orbitals, leaving **two electrons unpaired** (2p⁴ → ↑↑↑↓).  

*Molecular oxygen* (MO configuration):  

(σ1s)² (σ*1s)² (σ2s)² (σ*2s)² (σ2p)² (π2p)⁴ (π*2p)¹ (π*2p)¹  

The two highest‑energy electrons occupy the degenerate π* antibonding orbitals with parallel spins, giving **two unpaired electrons** in the π* set.  Thus O₂ is a triplet ground state.

---

**c. Energy of the excited singlet state of O₂ (λ = 1270 nm)**  

\[
E = \frac{hc}{\lambda}
   = \frac{(6.62607015\times10^{-34}\ \text{J·s})(2.99792458\times10^{8}\ \text{m·s}^{-1})}
          {1.270\times10^{-6}\ \text{m}}
   = 1.564\times10^{-19}\ \text{J per photon}
\]

\[
E_{\text{mol}} = (1.564\times10^{-19}\ \text{J})(6.02214076\times10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1})
               = 9.42\times10^{4}\ \text{J mol}^{-1}
               \approx \boxed{94\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}}
\]

---

**d. Why O₂ does not absorb IR light whereas O₃ does**  

A molecule can absorb IR radiation only if a vibrational mode produces a change in its dipole moment.  O₂ is homonuclear; all its vibrational motions are symmetric with respect to the centre of charge, so the dipole moment remains zero (or unchanged) and the transitions are **IR‑inactive**.  

O₃ is a bent (C₂ᵥ) molecule with a permanent dipole moment.  Its normal modes (especially the asymmetric stretch) change the dipole moment, making them **IR‑active**.  Consequently O₃ absorbs IR light, while O₂ does not.

---

**e. O–O bond distances for the six oxygen species**

| Species | O–O distance (pm) | Reasoning (bond‑order / electron‑repulsion) |
|---------|-------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| O₂⁺ (dioxygenyl cation) | **112** | Removal of an electron from the π* antibonding orbital raises the bond order to 2.5 → shortest bond. |
| O₂ (dioxygen) | **121** | Neutral O₂ has bond order 2 (one σ + one π bond). |
| O₃ (ozone) | **127 – 128** | Ozone has two equivalent O–O bonds with bond order ≈ 1.5 (three‑centre four‑electron bonds). |
| O₂⁻ (superoxide) | **128 – 127** (essentially same as O₃) | One extra electron in a π* orbital lowers bond order to 1.5, lengthening the bond relative to O₂, but the length is still close to that of ozone. |
| O₃⁻ (ozonide) | **135** | Adding an electron to ozone occupies an antibonding orbital, further weakening the O–O bonds; the O–O distance is noticeably longer than in O₃. |
| O₂²⁻ (peroxide) | **154** | The peroxide ion has a single O–O σ bond (bond order = 1) and maximum electron‑pair repulsion, giving the longest O–O separation. |

*Note:* The two values 127 pm and 128 pm are treated as essentially identical; they are assigned to O₃ and O₂⁻, whose bond lengths are predicted to be very similar.  The ordering from shortest to longest follows the expected decrease in bond order and increase in electron‑repulsion as electrons are added to antibonding orbitals.

It adopts a cubic perovskite unit cell with three visually distinct sphere types: small gray spheres at the eight cube corners, medium white spheres at the six face centers, and one large black sphere at the body center. Count atoms using normal crystallographic fractional occupancy of corners and faces.
a. Which element corresponds to the small gray spheres, which to the medium sized white spheres, and which to the large black spheres?
b. Describe the coordination number and the identity of the nearest neighbor atoms for each of the types of atoms in CsPbI3.
c. The length of the unit cell edge in CsPbI3 is 628 pm. What is the density of CsPbI3, in g cm-3?

Its unit cell diagram uses four visually distinct sphere types. Staticized diagram description: type A spheres appear once per unit cell in the central layer; type B spheres appear twice per unit cell in layers above and below the central layer; type C black spheres appear in three crystallographically distinct positions, with one in the middle layer and two on the top and bottom faces; type D small spheres appear seven times per unit cell. The type C sites on the top and bottom faces each have four nearest type D neighbors arranged at the corners of an approximately flat square. The middle-layer type C sites have those four near-coplanar type D neighbors plus one additional nearest type D neighbor along the vertical axis.
d. Identify which elements correspond to the four types of spheres in the diagram.
e. Give the oxidation numbers of each element in YBa2Cu3O7.
f. The atoms represented by the black spheres have two different coordination geometries in the structure shown. What are the geometries? How is this observation related to the oxidation numbers you determined in part e?

turns.candidate_answer:
**a. Identification of the spheres in CsPbI₃**

In the cubic perovskite cell the atoms occupy the positions:

* **Corners** – one Cs⁺ ion per corner (shared by eight cells) → 1 Cs per cell.  
* **Body centre** – one Pb²⁺ ion → 1 Pb per cell.  
* **Face centres** – three I⁻ ions (one on each of three alternate faces) → 3 I per cell.

The description “small gray spheres at the eight cube corners” therefore refers to **Cs**, the “medium white spheres at the six face centres” refers to **I**, and the “one large black sphere at the body centre” refers to **Pb**.

---

**b. Coordination numbers and nearest‑neighbour identities**

| Atom | Position in the cell | Coordination number | Nearest‑neighbour atoms (first coordination sphere) |
|------|---------------------|----------------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| **Cs** | corner (0,0,0) | 12 | 12 I⁻ ions (the 12 I atoms that lie at the face‑centres of the six faces surrounding the corner) |
| **Pb** | body centre (½,½,½) | 6 | 6 I⁻ ions (the octahedron of I atoms that surround the body centre) |
| **I**  | face centre (e.g., ½,½,0) | 6 | 2 Pb²⁺ ions (the two Pb atoms that lie on either side of the face, distance = a/2) **and** 4 Cs⁺ ions (the four Cs atoms at the corners of that face, distance = a/√2).  The two Pb atoms are the closest, but the full first coordination sphere includes the four Cs atoms as well. |

---

**c. Density of CsPbI₃**

*Edge length* \(a = 628\ \text{pm} = 6.28\times10^{-8}\ \text{cm}\)  
*Volume of the unit cell* \(V = a^{3} = (6.28\times10^{-8})^{3}=2.48\times10^{-22}\ \text{cm}^{3}\)

*Molar mass*  
\[
M(\text{CsPbI}_{3}) = 132.91\ (\text{Cs}) + 207.2\ (\text{Pb}) + 3(126.90)\ (\text{I})
                     \approx 720.8\ \text{g mol}^{-1}
\]

*Mass of one formula unit*  
\[
m = \frac{M}{N_{\!A}} = \frac{720.8\ \text{g mol}^{-1}}{6.022\times10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}}
    = 1.20\times10^{-21}\ \text{g}
\]

*Density*  
\[
\rho = \frac{m}{V}
      = \frac{1.20\times10^{-21}\ \text{g}}{2.48\times10^{-22}\ \text{cm}^{3}}
      \approx 4.8\ \text{g cm}^{-3}
\]

\[
\boxed{\rho_{\text{CsPbI}_{3}} \approx 4.8\ \text{g cm}^{-3}}
\]

---

**d. Identification of the four sphere types in YBa₂Cu₃O₇**

The formula contains one Y, two Ba, three Cu and seven O atoms per unit cell.  
The description matches these stoichiometric numbers:

* **Type A** (appears once in the central layer) → **Y**  
* **Type B** (appears twice in the layers above and below) → **Ba**  
* **Type C** (appears three times: one in the middle layer and two on the top/bottom faces) → **Cu**  
* **Type D** (appears seven times) → **O**

---

**e. Oxidation numbers in YBa₂Cu₃O₇**

* Y is a Group 13 metal → **+3**  
* Ba is an alkaline earth metal → **+2**  
* O is the most electronegative element → **–2**

Let the (average) oxidation state of Cu be \(x\):

\[
(+3) + 2(+2) + 3x + 7(-2) = 0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
3 + 4 + 3x - 14 = 0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
3x = +7
\;\Longrightarrow\;
x = +\frac{7}{3}\ (\approx +2.33)
\]

Thus the copper atoms are in a mixed‑valent state: two Cu atoms are **+2** and one Cu atom is **+3** (total charge from Cu = +7).

\[
\boxed{\text{Y: }+3,\ \text{Ba: }+2,\ \text{Cu: }+7/3\ (\text{two }+2,\ \text{one }+3),\ \text{O: }-2}
\]

---

**f. Coordination geometries of the copper atoms and their relation to oxidation state**

The black spheres (Cu) occupy two crystallographically distinct sites:

1. **Square planar** – the Cu atoms on the top and bottom faces (the “chain” Cu). Each has four nearest‑neighbour O atoms arranged at the corners of an approximately flat square.  
2. **Square pyramidal** – the Cu atom in the middle layer (the “plane” Cu). It has the four coplanar O neighbours plus one additional O atom along the vertical axis, giving a square‑pyramidal environment.

**Relation to oxidation numbers:**  
* Cu⁺ (d¹⁰) is usually linear or tetrahedral.  
* Cu²⁺ (d⁹) is subject to Jahn–Teller distortion and commonly adopts a **square‑pyramidal** (or distorted octahedral) geometry.  
* Cu³⁺ (d⁸) strongly favours a **square‑planar** geometry.

The observed square‑planar Cu is therefore the Cu³⁺ ion, while the square‑pyramidal Cu is the Cu²⁺ ion. This directly confirms the mixed oxidation state (+2 and +3) deduced from the overall charge balance in part (e).

**a.  Bromination of 3‑methylpentane**

*Conditions* – Exposure of the alkane to Br₂ under UV light (or at elevated temperature) starts a radical chain reaction.  
Because the C‑3 carbon of 3‑methylpentane is **tertiary**, the tertiary‑alkyl radical that is formed is the most stable, so bromination occurs almost exclusively at that carbon.

*Product* – 3‑bromo‑3‑methylpentane  

```
           Br
            |
CH₃ – CH₂ – C – CH₂ – CH₃
            |
           CH₃
```

(Empirical formula C₆H₁₃Br, single monobromide.)

**b.  Cyclohexene + Br₂ in two different solvents**

| Solvent | Reaction | Product (with stereochemistry) |
|---------|----------|--------------------------------|
| **CCl₄** (non‑polar) | Electrophilic addition of Br₂ → a cyclic bromonium ion that is opened by Br⁻ **anti** to the C–C bond. | **trans‑1,2‑dibromocyclohexane** – the two Br atoms end up on opposite faces of the ring (one wedge, one dash). |
| **H₂O** (polar, nucleophilic) | The bromonium ion is opened by the nucleophile **H₂O**; the result is a bromohydrin. The addition is again **anti**, giving the OH and Br trans to each other. | **trans‑1‑bromo‑2‑hydroxycyclohexane** (a bromohydrin) – the Br and OH are on opposite sides of the ring. |

---

**c.  Bromination of benzene**

*Catalyst* – A Lewis acid that can coordinate to Br₂, e.g. **FeBr₃** (or AlCl₃, FeCl₃).  

*Major product* – **Bromobenzene**  

```
   Br
   |
   │
  ╱╲
 ╱  ╲
│    │
 ╲  ╱
  ╲╱
   ⬡
```

(The benzene ring retains its aromatic sextet; the Br is attached directly to the ring.)

---

**d.  Cyclopentanone + excess Br₂ / base → tetrabromide**

*Product* – **2,2,5,5‑tetrabromocyclopentanone**  

```
      O
      ‖
   C‑(CBr₂)‑CH₂‑CH₂‑(CBr₂)‑   (five‑membered ring)
```

The carbonyl carbon is C‑1; C‑2 and C‑5 each bear **two Br atoms** (gem‑dibromination), giving the tetrabromide.

*Why monobromide is not obtained even with one equivalent of Br₂*  

1. **Base‑catalysed enolisation** – the first deprotonation gives an enolate that reacts rapidly with Br₂ to give the α‑bromo ketone.  
2. **Inductive effect of the newly introduced Br** – the bromine strongly withdraws electron density, making the remaining α‑hydrogen on the same carbon **much more acidic** (pKₐ drops).  
3. **Enolate re‑formation is faster** – the enhanced acidity causes the enolate to be regenerated more readily, so a second bromination (gem‑dibromination) occurs before the monobromo product can be isolated.  
4. **Same reasoning applies to the other α‑carbon**; thus the reaction proceeds to the **tetrabromo** species even when only one equivalent of Br₂ is present. Consequently, the yield of the monobromide is very low.

---

**e.  Acetophenone + excess I₂ / NaOH (iodoform test)**  

The reaction is the **iodoform (halo‑form) reaction** of a methyl ketone.

*Yellow precipitate* – **Iodoform, CHI₃**  

```
    I
    |
I‑C‑I
    |
    H
```

*Water‑soluble organic product* – **Benzoate ion (as Na⁺ salt)**  

```
   O⁻
   ‖
C₆H₅‑C
   O⁻
```

(Neutral form would be benzoic acid; under the basic conditions it exists as sodium benzoate, C₆H₅COONa.)

Overall halo‑form equation for acetophenone:

\[
\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3 + 3\,I_2 + 4\,OH^- \longrightarrow C_6H_5COO^- + CHI_3 + 3\,I^- + 3\,H_2O}
\]
